evidence.quote: The CWMs framework is an exciting direction for model-based planning, but we still rely on limiting assumptions of deterministic and fully observable environments.

Another potential issue is providing a description of the environment that can be reasonably converted to a Python function (e.g. a manual documenting key variables) when such a description is not available (e.g. when the environment is defined with image observations).

CWMs struggle especially on complex physics-based environments; thus a promising direction could also be allowing programs generated by GIF-MCTS to make use of external tools and libraries, such as physics simulators.
We leave more thorough experiments on sample efficiency for CWM agents to future work.
For budget constraints, we run a single random seed for each ablation and compare with a single GIF-MCTS run with the same random seed.

We have validated the GIF-MCTS approach as an efficient code synthesis method, with the key limiting assumption of having available test cases to evaluate code, which could be difficult to provide in certain tasks.
Both stochasticity and partial observability would pose challenges, especially on the verification of the CWM prediction, as there is no set result for a given input.
We further experiment with a higher number of LLM calls for GPT-4 Turbo, matching the one used for Llama 3, as we couldn’t do this on the full CWMB due to budget concerns.

This is often due to the incorrect prediction of terminal states: these are rarer in the replay buffer, especially states that terminate with a success/positive reward. This can cause the planning algorithm to fail, as it is missing the reward signal.
As the code generated by the LLM is untrusted, it should always be checked by a human expert before it is used under any circumstances.
